extracted.intended_audience: educators, curriculum designers, policymakers, and media-literacy practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for developing and assessing core social skills and cultural competencies that enable youth to participate in participatory/digital media culture; intended to inform classroom, after-school, and parent practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play
rubrics_metrics.description: The capacity to experiment with the surroundings as a form of problem solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage open-ended exploration and experimentation as a learning strategy; value personal meaning and intrinsic motivation in student projects (linked to constructivist principles and Computer Clubhouse practices). Examples: experimental simulations, exploratory production activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to adopt alternative identities for the purpose of improvisation and discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use role-play and identity-based exercises to foster improvisation and discovery (e.g., adopting personas in literature or social studies activities). Helps students explore perspective-taking and creative expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to interpret and construct dynamic models of real-world processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to build, run, and critique simulations as models of complex phenomena (e.g., scientific models, city-planning simulations). Use simulation tools to link classroom inquiry to real-world processes and decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to meaningfully sample and remix media content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess students on their ability to select, transform, and integrate existing media into new works while understanding legal/ethical contexts. Classroom activities: remix projects, appropriation in literature classes; evaluate meaningfulness of sampling and remix choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multitasking
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to scan the environment and shift focus onto salient details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value skills in managing attention across multiple information streams and prioritizing salient content. Instructional design should scaffold how to monitor multiple sources without losing depth of understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributed cognition
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to interact meaningfully with tools that expand mental capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how students use external tools (software, databases, collaborative platforms) to extend thinking and problem-solving. Encourage fluency with information appliances and collaborative technologies that distribute cognitive work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to pool knowledge and compare notes with others toward a common goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess participation in collaborative knowledge production and the quality of synthesis. Draw on Surowiecki’s four qualities of smart crowds—diversity, decentralization, aggregation (a way of summarizing opinions), and independence—and teach how these conditions affect the reliability and usefulness of collective outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to evaluate the reliability and credibility of different information sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should learn to assess motives, provenance, accuracy, and bias of sources; choose trusted, unbiased, third‑party assessments when appropriate; instructors can model source selection strategies and scaffold credibility checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmedia navigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to follow the flow of stories and information across multiple modalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to track narratives and information as they move across platforms (text, video, games, social media) and to understand relations between media systems. Evaluate their ability to synthesize cross‑modal information and select appropriate tools for different modalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Networking
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to search for, synthesize, and disseminate information across social communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes (a) identifying which group/community is most aware of relevant resources and selecting search systems matched to criteria (similar tastes, viewpoints, divergent perspectives, goals, popularity, trusted third parties); (b) sampling and distilling multiple independent perspectives into meaningful synthesis rather than copying large blocks of text; and (c) effectively tapping social networks to distribute students’ own media and increase visibility (e.g., web rings, blogs, podcasts). Examples: Webquests for structured research; guidance on ethical/public consequences of publishing to larger audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to travel across diverse communities, discerning and respecting multiple perspectives, and grasping and following alternative norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes active listening, ethical principles for mutual respect, agreed rules of conduct, deliberation over adversarial debate, and the capacity to 'disagree agreeably.' Classroom practices: structured deliberation, projects that bring diverse groups together (Stanford Center for Deliberative Democracy model, Cultura Project), forum-based cross-cultural exchanges, and exercises that surface norms and values. Evaluate capacity to deliberate, find compromise or agree to disagree, and reformulate positions after listening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share/Jolls/Thoman media-literacy inquiry framework
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of core inquiry questions for critically analyzing media messages: Who created the message? What creative techniques are used to attract my attention? How may different people understand this message differently than me? What lifestyles, values, and points of view are represented in—or omitted from—this message? Why is this message being sent?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report praises these questions but advises reframing them to incorporate active participation (i.e., recognizing that students also create and circulate media). Use these questions as a reusable analytic rubric across media forms; extend them to prompt students to reflect on their own role as producers, not just recipients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrated media-pedagogy components (technical skills, exemplars, expressions, ethics)
rubrics_metrics.description: An instructional approach combining: (a) exercises that introduce technical skills and cultural competencies; (b) exemplars that teach critical analysis of existing media texts; (c) production activities that encourage students to create new media; and (d) ethics that prompt reflection on consequences of media-making choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogy should not treat media literacy as an add-on but integrate it across disciplines. After‑school programs should emphasize experimentation and technical skill-building; schools should incorporate evaluation and contextualization of student work. Parents, museums, libraries, and community organizations are stakeholders in supporting these components. Assess students on technical proficiency, critical analysis, quality of produced media, and ethical reasoning about public consequences.
